readings.c1s2:
¶
'''Wildcat engine.''' See ''engine.''

'''wildebeest''' (wil′de-bāst), ''n.'' [D., = E. ''wild beast.''] The gnu. [South Africa.]

'''wilder''' (wil′dėr), ''v. t.'' [A freq. form, < ''wild'', ''a.'', prob. suggested by ''wilderness'', and as to form by ''wander''. Hence ''bewilder''.] To cause to lose the way or track; puzzle with mazes or difficulties; bewilder.

{{smaller block|So that it ''wilderd'' and lost it selfe in those many by-waies.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 364.}}
<poem>We are a widow’s three poor sons,
Lang ''wilder’d'' on the sea.</poem>
{{right|''Rosmer Hafmand'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 254).}}
<poem>When red morn
Made paler the pale moon, to her cold home,
''Wildered'' and wan and panting, she returned.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Alastor.}}}}

'''wilderedly''' (wil′dėrd-li), ''adv.'' [< ''wildered'', pp., + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In a wildered manner; bewilderedly; wildly; incoherently.

{{smaller block|<poem>It is but in thy passion and thy heat
Thou speak’st so ''wilderedly.''</poem>
{{right|''Sir H. Taylor'', Isaac Comnenus, ii. 2.}}}}

'''wildering''' (wīl′dėr-ing), ''n.'' Same as ''wilding''.

'''wilderment''' (wil′dėr-ment), ''n.'' [< ''wilder'' + ''-ment''. Cf. ''bewilderment''.] Bewilderment; confusion. [Poetical.]

{{smaller block|<poem>This ''wilderment'' of wreck and death.</poem>
{{right|''Moore'', Lalla Rookh, The Fire Worshippers.}}
So in ''wilderment'' of gazing I looked up, and I looked down.
{{right|''Mrs. Browning'', Lost Bower, st. 57.}}}}

'''wildern†''', ''n.'' [ME., also ''wilderne''; prob. < AS. *''wildern'', < ''wilder'', a reduced form of ''wildeór'', ''wild deór'', a wild beast: see ''wild''<sup>1</sup> and ''deer''. Cf. ''wilderness''.] A wilderness.

'''4.''' In ''coal-mining'', the name formerly sometimes given by miners to fire-damp.—'''5.''' Erysipelas; also, lichen circumscriptus, an eruptive disease, consisting of clusters or patches of papulæ.
{{smaller block|A ''wylde fyr'' upon thair bodyes falle.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve’s Tale, l. 252.}}}}

'''6.''' A disease of sheep, attended with inflammation of the skin.—{{smaller|'''Wild-fire rash''', a skin eruption, usually of infants only, consisting of papules arranged in circumscribed patches appearing in succession on different parts of the body; strophulus volaticus.}}

'''wild-flying''' (wīld′flī″ing), ''a.'' Flighty.
{{smaller block|<poem>If any thing redeem the emperor
From his ''wild-flying'' courses, this is she.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Valentinian, i. 2.}}}}

'''wild-fowl''' (wīld′foul), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wylde fowle'', ''wyyldefowle'', < AS. ''wild-fugel'', wild fowl: see ''wild''<sup>1</sup> and ''fowl''<sup>1</sup>.] The birds of the duck tribe collectively considered; the ''Anatidæ''; water-fowl: sometimes extended to other birds ordinarily pursued as game.

'''wildgrave''' (wīld′grāv), ''n.'' [= G. ''wildgraf''; < ''wild'', game, + ''graf'', count: see ''wild''<sup>1</sup> and ''grave''<sup>5</sup>.] The title of various German counts or nobles whose office originally was connected with the forests or with hunting.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''Wildgrave'' winds his bugle-horn,
To horse, to horse! halloo, halloo!</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Wild Huntsman.}}}}

'''wilding''' (wīl′ding), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ''wild''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>3</sup>.] '''I.''' ''n.'' A plant that is wild or that grows without cultivation; specifically, a wild crab-apple tree; also, the fruit of such a plant.

{{smaller block|<poem>And ''wildings'' or the seasons fruite
He did in scrip bestow.</poem>
{{right|''Warner'', Albion’s England, iv. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A choice dish of ''wildings'' here, to scald
And mingle with your cream.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Sad Shepherd, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Matthew is in his grave, yet now
Me thinks I see him stand
As at that moment, with a bough
Of ''wilding'' in his hand.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Two April Mornings (1799).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A leafless ''wilding'' shivering by the wall.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Under the Willows.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Wild; not cultivated or domesticated. [Poetical.]
{{smaller block|<poem>O ''wilding'' rose, whom fancy thus endears,
I bid your blossoms in my bonnet wave.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Whose field of life, by angels sown,
The ''wilding'' vines o’erran.</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', William Forster.}}}}

'''wildish''' (wīl′dish), ''a.'' [< ''wild''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Somewhat wild.
{{smaller block|He is a little ''wildish'', they say.
{{right|''Richardson'', Pamela, I. xxxii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>’Twould be a ''wildish'' destiny
If we, who thus together roam
In a strange Land and far from home,
Were in this place the guests of Chance.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Stepping Westward.}}}}

'''wildness''' (wīld′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wyldenesse'', ''wildnesse'' (cf. G. ''wildniss'', desert, wilderness); < ''wild''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness''.] '''1.''' The state or character of being wild, in any sense.
{{smaller block|<poem>The perelle of youth for to pace
Withoute ony deth or distresse,
It is so fulle of ''wyldenesse''.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 4894.}}
<poem>Wilder to him than tigers in their ''wildness''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 980.}}
Take heed, sir; be not madder than you would make him: Though he be rash and sudden (which is all his ''wildness''), Take heed you wrong him not. ''Fletcher'', Pilgrim, v. 5.}}
'''2†.''' A wild place or country; a wilderness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thise tyraunts put hem gladly not in pres,
No ''wildnesse'' ne no busshes for to winne.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Former Age, l. 34.}}}}

'''Wild’s case.''' See ''case''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wild-williams''' (wīld-wil′yamz), ''n.'' An old name of the ragged-robin, ''Lychnis Flos-cuculi.''

'''wild-wind†''' (wīld′wind), ''n.'' A hurricane.
{{smaller block|In the year of our Lord 1639, in November, here happened an hirecano or ''wild-wind''. ''Fuller'', Worthies, I. 495.}}

'''wild-wood''' (wīld′wu̇d), ''n.'' and ''a.'' '''I.''' ''n.'' The wild, unfrequented woods; a forest.
{{smaller block|The orchard, the meadow, the deep tangled ''wild-wood''.
{{right|''S. Woodworth'', The Old Oaken Bucket.}}}}

'''II.''' ''a.'' Belonging to wild, uncultivated, or unfrequented woods. [Poetical.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Aye the ''wild-wood'' echoes rang—
Oh, dearly do I love thee, Annie!</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', By Allan Stream.}}}}

'''wile'''<sup>1</sup> (wīl), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wile'', ''wyle'', < AS. ''wīl'', ''wile'' (also in comp. ''flyge-wīl'', ‘a flying wile,’ an arrow); cf. Icel. ''vēl'', ''væl'', an artifice, wile, craft, device, fraud, trick (> OF. ''guile'', > E. ''guile'': see ''guile''<sup>1</sup>).] A trick or stratagem; anything practised for insnaring or deception; a sly, insidious artifice.
{{smaller block|<poem>Bot hit is no ferly, thaȝ a fole madde,
And thurȝ ''wyles'' of wymmen be wonen to sorȝe.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2415.}}}}
{{smaller block|Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the ''wiles'' of the devil. {{right|Eph. vi. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Quips, and cranks, and wanton ''wiles'',
Nods, and becks, and wreathed smiles,
Such as hang on Hebe’s cheek.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', L’Allegro, l. 27.}}}}

='''Syn.''' ''Manœuver'', ''Stratagem'', etc. See ''artifice''.

'''wile'''<sup>1</sup> (wīl), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wiled'', ppr. ''wiling''. [< ''wile''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] '''1†.''' To deceive; beguile; impose on.
{{smaller block|<poem>So perfect in that art was Paridell
That he Malbeccoes halfen eye did ''wyle;''
His halfen eye he ''wiled'' wondrous well.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. x. 5.}}}}

'''2.''' To lure; entice; inveigle; coax; cajole.
{{smaller block|<poem>Say, whence is yond warlow with his wand,
That thus wold ''wyle'' oure folk away?</poem>
{{right|''Towneley Mysteries'', p. 60.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>She ''wiled'' him into ae chamber,
She ''wiled'' him into twa.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Hugh, or the Jew’s Daughter'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 332).}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wildcat|6925|wilful}}</noinclude>''Felis'' and ''Lynx''; especially, in North America, the bay lynx (''L. rufus'') and Canada lynx (''L. canadensis''), and sometimes the cougar (''F. concolor''). See ''cat''<sup>1</sup>, and cuts under ''cougar'' and ''lynx''.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Wild; reckless; haphazard: applied especially to unsound business enterprises: as, ''wildcat'' banking (see below); ''wildcat'' currency (currency issued by a wildcat bank); a ''wildcat'' scheme (a reckless, unstable venture); ''wildcat'' stock (stock of some wildcat or unsound company or organization). [Colloq., U. S.]
{{smaller block|The first night of our journey was spent at Ashford, in Connecticut, where we arrived late in the evening; and here the bother of ''wild-cat'' currency, as it was afterward called, was forced upon our attention.
{{right|''Josiah Quincy'', Figures of the Past, p. 196.}}}}
{{smaller block|The present system, though an immense improvement in every respect on the heterogeneous old breed of State and ''wild-cat'' banks that wrought ruin in 1836 and 1857, is nevertheless of the same dangerous character.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXLI. 199.}}}}

'''Wildcat banking''', a name given, especially in the western United States, to the operations of organizations or individuals who, under the loose State banking-laws which prevailed before the passage of the National Bank Act of 1863, issued large amounts of bank-notes though possessing little or no capital.
{{smaller block|The ''wild-cat banking'' which devastated the Ohio States between 1837 and 1860, and miseducated the people of those States until they thought irredeemable government issues an unhoped-for blessing, never could have existed if Story’s opinion had been law.
{{right|''W. G. Sumner'', Andrew Jackson, p. 363.}}}}

{{right|''Reliquiæ Antiquæ'', I. 130.}}}}
'''wilderness''' (wil′dėr-nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wildernesse, wyldernys'' (= MD. ''wildernisse''); < ''wildern'' (or the orig. AS. ''wilder'') + ''-ness.'']   '''1.''' A tract of land inhabited only by wild beasts; a desert, whether forest or plain.
{{smaller block|And after that Men comen out of Surreye, and entren in to ''Wyldernesse,'' and there the Weye is sondy.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ich wente forth wyde-where walkynge myn one,
In a wylde ''wyldernesse'' by a wode-syde.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xi. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O for a lodge in some vast ''wilderness,''
Some boundless contiguity of shade!</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, ii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' A wild; a waste of any kind.
{{smaller block|<poem>Environ’d with a ''wilderness'' of sea.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iii. 1. 94.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The watery ''wilderness'' yields no supply.</poem>
{{right|''Waller'', Instruction to a Painter.}}}}
'''3.''' A part of a garden set apart for plants to grow in with unchecked luxuriance.   ''Imp. Dict.'' —'''4.''' A confused or bewildering mass, heap, or collection.
{{smaller block|<poem>Rome is but a ''wilderness'' of tigers.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tit. And., iii. 1. 54.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The land thou hast left a ''wilderness'' of wretches.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Bonduca, v. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Flowering odours, cassia, nard, and balm;
A ''wilderness'' of sweets.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., v. 294.}}}}
'''5†.''' Wildness.
{{smaller block|<poem>Such a warped slip of ''wilderness''
Ne’er issued from his blood.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 1. 142.}}}} 435 {{smaller block|<poem>These paths and bowers doubt not but our joint hands
Will keep from ''wilderness'' with ease.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 245.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' ''Wilderness, Desert.'' See ''desert''<sup>1</sup>.

'''Wilde’s incision.''' In ''otology'', a free incision down to the bone over the mastoid process, made in certain cases of disease of the ear.

'''wild-fire''' (wīld′fīr), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''wylde fyer, wylde fyre''; < ME. ''wilde fir, wylde fyyr, wylde fyr, wilde fur, wylde fur''; < ''wild''<sup>1</sup> + ''fire''.]   '''1.''' A composition of inflammable materials readily catching fire and hard to be extinguished; Greek fire: often used figuratively.
{{smaller block|<poem>Faith his sheild must be
To quench the balles of ''wilde-fyer'' presentlie.</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 145.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Balls of ''wildfire'' may be safely touch’d,
Not violently sunder’d and thrown up.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Lover’s Melancholy, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|I was at that time rich in fame — for my book ran like ''wild-fire.'' {{right|''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, xxx.}}}}
'''2.''' Sheet-lightning; a kind of lightning unaccompanied by thunder.
{{smaller block|What is called “summer lightning” or “''wild-fire''” is sometimes a rather puzzling phenomenon.
{{right|''P. G. Tait'', Encyc. Brit., XXIII. 330.}}}}
'''3†.''' The blue flames of alcohol burnt in some dishes when brought on table, as with plum-pudding.
{{smaller block|Swiche manere bake-metes and dissh-metes brennynge of ''wilde fir'', and peynted and castelled with papir.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}

'''4.''' In ''coal-mining'', the name formerly sometimes given by miners to fire-damp.—'''5.''' Erysipelas; also, lichen circumscriptus, an eruptive disease, consisting of clusters or patches of papulæ.
{{smaller block|A ''wylde fyr'' upon thair bodyes falle.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve’s Tale, l. 252.}}}}

'''6.''' A disease of sheep, attended with inflammation of the skin.—{{smaller|'''Wild-fire rash''', a skin eruption, usually of infants only, consisting of papules arranged in circumscribed patches appearing in succession on different parts of the body; strophulus volaticus.}}

='''Syn.''' ''Manœuver'', ''Stratagem'', etc. See ''artifice''.

'''wile'''<sup>1</sup> (wīl), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wiled'', ppr. ''wiling''.   [< ''wile''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''1†.''' To deceive; beguile; impose on.
{{smaller block|<poem>So perfect in that art was Paridell
That he Malbeccoes halfen eye did ''wyle;''
His halfen eye he ''wiled'' wondrous well.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. x. 5.}}}}

'''2.''' To lure; entice; inveigle; coax; cajole.
{{smaller block|<poem>Say, whence is yond warlow with his wand,
That thus wold ''wyle'' oure folk away?</poem>
{{right|''Towneley Mysteries'', p. 60.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>She ''wiled'' him into ae chamber,
She ''wiled'' him into twa.</poem>
{{right|''Sir Hugh, or the Jew’s Daughter'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 332).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But court na anither, tho’ jokin’ ye be,
For fear that she ''wile'' your fancy frae me.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Oh Whistle and I’ll Come to you.}}}}
'''3.''' To shorten or cause to pass easily or pleasantly, as by some diverting wile: in this sense probably confused with ''while.''
{{smaller block|Seated in two black horsehair porter’s chairs, one on each side of the fireplace, the superannuated Mr. and Mrs. Smallweed ''wile'' away the rosy hours.
{{right|''Dickens'', Bleak House, xxi.}}}}

'''wile<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''while''<sup>1</sup>.

'''wile<sup>3</sup>†''', ''n.'' Same as ''wild''<sup>2</sup>, ''Weald'' (?).
{{smaller block|The earth is the Lords, and all the corners thereof; he created the mountaines of Wales as well as the ''wiles'' of Kent. {{right|''Howell'', Forreine Travell (ed. Arber), p. 29.}}}}

'''wilful, willful''' (wil′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wilful, wilfull, wylfulle, willfulle''; < ''will''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', + ''-ful.'']   '''1†.''' Willing; ready; eager; keen.
{{smaller block|<poem>With his ferefull folke to Phocus hee rides,
And is ''wilfull'' in werk to wirchen hem care.</poem>
{{right|''Alisaunder of Macedoine'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 412.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As thai past on the payment the pepull beheld,
Haden wonder of the weghes, & ''wilfulde'' desyre
To know of there comyng and the cause wete,
That were so rially arait & a rowte gay.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 353.}}}}
{{smaller block|When walls are so ''wilful'' to hear without warning.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., v. 1. 211.}}}}
'''2.''' Due to one’s own will; spontaneous; voluntary; deliberate; intentional: as, ''wilful'' murder; ''wilful'' waste.
{{smaller block|Alle the sones of Israel halewiden ''wilful'' thingis [brought a willing offering, A.V.] to the Lord.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Ex. xxxv. 29.}}}}
<poem>The hye God on whom that we bileeve
In ''wilful'' poverte chees to lyve his lyf.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Wife of Bath’s Tale, l. 323.}}}}
